So dyslexia is a language-based learning disability. Students with dyslexia usually experience difficulties with spelling, writing, and pronouncing words.

problems with how you store words and their meanings in the memory, as well as trouble forming sentences to communicate more complex ideas. Dyslexia falls under the umbrella of specific learning disorder. The disorder has three main subtypes for reading, writing, and math.

As a child gets older, dyslexia can often look like difficulty spelling simple words, learning to speak, learning letters and their sounds, troubles learning the names of the letters, problems telling letters apart, such as B or D, and P and Q, trouble rhyming, reluctant to read aloud in class, trouble sounding out new words, trouble learning how sounds go together, mixing up the position of sounds and words, organizing written and spoken language, memorizing number facts, reading quickly enough

to comprehend, understanding longer assignments that are required, spelling, learning a foreign language, and even correctly doing math problems. Having one of the above doesn't necessarily mean a child will have dyslexia, but if they're having trouble learning some of the basic reading skills, then it's recommended that a dyslexia screening and test is a good way to see if specialized help is needed.

The impact that dyslexia has is different from each person and depends on the severity of the condition, as well as the effectiveness of the instruction or remediation, ranging from mild, moderate, to severe. Students with dyslexia may find it difficult to express themselves clearly or to fully comprehend what others mean when they speak.

Such language problems are often difficult to recognize, but they can lead to major problems in school, in the workplace, as well as relating to other people. Having dyslexia is not a measure of intelligence, however, dyslexia can affect a person's self-image.

Students with dyslexia also end up feeling sometimes dumb and less capable than their peers. After experiencing a great deal of stress due to academic problems, a student may become discouraged about continuing in school. Genetics play a role in having dyslexia as well. Dyslexia is a lifelong condition. With proper help, many people with dyslexia can learn to read and write very well. Early identification and treatment is the key to helping individuals with dyslexia achieve in school and in life.
